Making Appointments

A2 Business English lesson for arranging, changing and confirming appointments.

Start

Lesson overview

In this lesson, students learn simple language for making appointments at work, at a clinic, or on the phone.

Warm-up

When do you usually make appointments? Think about doctors, meetings, interviews, haircuts or school meetings.

Lesson aims

  • Ask if someone is available.
  • Suggest a day and time.
  • Accept or refuse politely.
  • Confirm appointment details.
  • Change an appointment.
Reading

Making an appointment

When you make an appointment, you agree on a day, a time and a place. You can make appointments by phone, by email, online or in person.

It is important to be polite and clear. First, explain why you need the appointment. Then ask about availability. If the first time is not possible, suggest another time.

At the end, confirm the details. You can say: So, that’s Tuesday at 10 o’clock. If you need to change the appointment later, apologise and ask for a new time.

Listening

Listening Comprehension: Making Appointments

Listen to the three appointment dialogues and answer the more detailed comprehension questions. Focus on reasons, changes, exact details and what each speaker confirms.

Listening answer key

  1. Michael is a returning patient because the receptionist already has his details / asks to check his phone number.
  2. Michael's phone number is 07855 249 631.
  3. He asks about Tuesday and Thursday.
  4. He accepts Thursday at 3 p.m.
  5. The receptionist tells him to arrive ten minutes early, probably so he can check in or update his details before the appointment.
  6. Emma says she has not trained at the gym before, so she is new to the gym.
  7. The available Monday time slots are 9 a.m., 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.
  8. Emma chooses 6 p.m., which suggests she is probably free later in the day.
  9. The session lasts one hour.
  10. It costs £25 for the training session.
  11. She needs to bring comfortable clothes and a water bottle; these are useful for exercising and staying hydrated.
  12. David's original appointment is on Friday at 4 p.m.
  13. He needs to change it because he has a work meeting.
  14. He changes it to Saturday.
  15. The new appointment is at 11 a.m.; it changes from Friday afternoon to Saturday morning.

Dialogue

Can we meet on Tuesday?

Anna: Good morning. I’d like to make an appointment with Mr Brown.

Receptionist: Of course. Are you available on Tuesday morning?

Anna: Sorry, Tuesday morning isn’t good for me. Do you have a slot in the afternoon?

Receptionist: Yes, we have 3 p.m.

Anna: That works for me.

Receptionist: Great. So, that’s Tuesday at 3 p.m.

Anna: Thank you. See you then.

Grammar

Would like / Can / Could

I’d like to... is polite: I’d like to make an appointment.

Can / Could are useful for requests: Can we meet on Monday? / Could I change the time?

Functional Language

Useful phrases

FunctionPhrase
Make an appointmentI’d like to make an appointment.
Ask availabilityAre you available on Monday?
Suggest a timeHow about Tuesday at 2?
AcceptThat works for me.
Refuse politelySorry, that time isn’t good for me.
ConfirmSo, that’s Wednesday at 10.
Speaking

Role play cards

Student A

Student B

You are the receptionist. You have free slots on Monday at 4 p.m. and Thursday at 10 a.m.

Student A

You need to reschedule a business meeting. Apologise and suggest a new time.

Student B

You are busy on Friday. Suggest Tuesday or Wednesday instead.

Speaking support

I’d like to make an appointment. / Are you available on...? / How about...? / That works for me. / Sorry, I need to reschedule.

Review

Final task

Write a short appointment message. Include: reason, day, time and confirmation.
